whatItFakes: The smallest change stored as a moment.
why: Defined as the smallest row of the 1967 scale (11 units) and carrying the 2021 replication's 22 as the other end of its spread (Oct 16, 2026). A yearly count of stored moments to check it against was not found, so the floor is a scale definition, not a calibrated count. Resolved Nov 10, 2026 (stand-in triage): dropped as too in depth (owner); the estimate stays as the game's answer.
replacement: Dropped Nov 10, 2026 (too in depth, owner): the estimate stays as the game's answer. Was: An owner answer or a tested calibration for the same quantity.

whatItFakes: The impact at which a moment takes over the screen.
why: A pacing choice by the owner, which no study measures (Oct 16, 2026 research); the marriage anchor is 50 units on both the 1967 scale and its 2021 replication, so the line holds if the scale is updated. Stays TUNABLE against play.
replacement: An owner answer or a tested calibration for the same quantity.

whatItFakes: How much the watched person's own death counts.
why: The watched person's own death is a design weight at the top of the scale; no stress scale rates one's own death (Oct 16, 2026 research). Stays TUNABLE against play.
replacement: An owner answer or a tested calibration for the same quantity.

whatItFakes: How much sociability raises a tie change.
why: Bounded above by the design's one quarter with 0 not contradicted (Oct 16, 2026 research: personality did not consistently moderate responses to life events). No coefficient exists. Resolved Nov 10, 2026 (stand-in triage): dropped as too in depth (owner); the estimate stays as the game's answer.
replacement: Dropped Nov 10, 2026 (too in depth, owner): the estimate stays as the game's answer. Was: An owner answer or a tested calibration for the same quantity.

whatItFakes: How much avoiding risk raises a money loss.
why: Bounded in size by the design's one quarter, sign from loss aversion, 0 not contradicted (Oct 16, 2026 research). No coefficient exists. Resolved Nov 10, 2026 (stand-in triage): dropped as too in depth (owner); the estimate stays as the game's answer.
replacement: Dropped Nov 10, 2026 (too in depth, owner): the estimate stays as the game's answer. Was: An owner answer or a tested calibration for the same quantity.

whatItFakes: When a contact is labeled a renewal (labeling only).
why: Labels a contact a renewal and decides no outcome; it follows from the half-lives (Oct 16, 2026 research). Stays TUNABLE. Resolved Nov 10, 2026 (stand-in triage): dropped as too in depth (owner); the estimate stays as the game's answer.
replacement: Dropped Nov 10, 2026 (too in depth, owner): the estimate stays as the game's answer. Was: An owner answer or a tested calibration for the same quantity.

whatItFakes: Standing ties for family and a shared home, the partner tie, and the fading discount.
why: The partner tie is now scaled from the spouse-to-close-family ratio on the 1967 scale (0.79; 0.57 on the 2021 replication). No source ranks sibling, grandparent, grandchild or shared-home ties or measures the fading discount; they stay the October 8, 2026 design weights until the replay calibration.
replacement: A calibration of thread importance against recorded closeness in replayed lives.

whatItFakes: How fast closeness fades without contact for friends and relatives.
why: No study reports a half-life for closeness without contact; Roberts and Dunbar (2015) give direction only, and 18 months is their study's length. Tagged TUNABLE (CTO, October 10, 2026). Resolved: Checked against Roberts and Dunbar (2015): their retention converts to 526 and 1,078 days, within 4 percent of 548 and 1,096; the kin value now equals the core's 1,095 and both rows carry the converted spread (Oct 16, 2026).
replacement: A half-life calibrated against network turnover over years (for example Mollenhorst, Volker and Flap 2014, once checked), the target P15 uses.

whatItFakes: The director recomputes each event's feeling with the core's exported appraisal function instead of reading the appraisal the core applied.
why: The core keeps only the resulting mood and stress (src/core2/modules/life.ts:319); hook requested from SOL-1258.
replacement: Read the appraisal receipt the core passes with each event.

whatItFakes: The director reads each watched person's tie changes once at the end of the day, so their order within the day is lost, although the core now sends a notice for each change.
why: Relationship changes emit no event (src/core2/state.ts:561); hook requested from SOL-1258.
replacement: A relationship change notice from the core.

whatItFakes: Favors and promises are kept-fact kinds with no producer, so a favor owed or a promise made is never remembered; lies are recorded.
why: The new core has no act or event that records a lie, a favor or a promise.
replacement: Producers in the core's conversation and favor modules, listed in producedBy.

whatItFakes: How fast an anniversary's weight falls away from the date.
why: The owner's answer 7. The only measured window is one week and no study calibrates the half-life (Oct 16, 2026 research).
replacement: A calibration against when people recall shared events.

whatItFakes: Impacts for recorded past facts, read from stress-scale rows rather than measured changes.
why: The eight past-fact weights are the 1967 Holmes and Rahe rows; the 2021 replication gives higher values for seven (carried as each row's spread). Choosing a vintage is the owner's call, since the floor and the interrupt line move with it. Resolved Nov 10, 2026 (stand-in triage): dropped as too in depth (owner); the estimate stays as the game's answer.
replacement: Dropped Nov 10, 2026 (too in depth, owner): the estimate stays as the game's answer. Was: Past moments measured from replayed lives once the life-replay harness runs on the new core.

whatItFakes: How long a watched person keeps every moment in full, and how many older moments they keep one by one.
why: No study sets either; chosen so memory stays about the same size across a year while the recent season stays whole.
replacement: A calibration against what people bring up in play (M4-05) and the owner's grading of the journal.

whatItFakes: The journal's line templates, written by hand instead of composed from mined real speech.

Resolved Oct 14 (words/mined-banks-in-play): the journal is worded from data/english/parts/journal.json via src/director/mined/journal-bank.ts; journal.json is deleted, its sentence-free rows live in journal-rows.json, and unworded moments are left out.
replacement: Lines composed from the mined first-person corpus in the speech research, refined by the owner's grades (M4-03).

whatItFakes: Conversation line templates written by hand instead of composed from mined real speech.
why: The first new-core conversations need words now; each template copies only recorded facts. Resolved Oct 14 (words/mined-banks-in-play): the director's conversation words are mined public-domain sentences from data/english/parts/conversation.json via src/director/mined/conversation-bank.ts; the hand-written bank is deleted and a moment no mined sentence covers is left unsaid.
replacement: Lines composed from the mined speech corpus and register cards, refined by the owner's grades (M4-02).

whatItFakes: Scene narration templates written by hand instead of composed from mined real speech and narration.
why: The first new-core scenes need words now; each template copies only recorded facts. Resolved Oct 14 (words/mined-banks-in-play): scenes are worded from data/english/parts/scene-words.json via src/director/mined/scene-bank.ts; scene-words.json is deleted and unmined settings are left unnarrated.
replacement: Narration composed from the mined corpus, refined by the owner's grades (M4-03).

whatItFakes: The filing clerk's line templates, written by hand instead of composed from mined real speech.

Resolved Oct 14 (words/mined-banks-in-play): the clerk speaks mined sentences from data/english/parts/filing-visit.json via src/director/mined/filing-bank.ts; filing-visit.json is deleted; fees and signatures stay record data and control names.

whatItFakes: The templates people use to bring up a change and say who caused it, and the one trait that sends blame toward authority.

Resolved Oct 14 (words/mined-banks-in-play): bring-it-up lines are mined from data/english/parts/bring-it-up.json via src/director/mined/scene-bank.ts; bring-it-up.json is deleted and the unmined told-blame line is left out.

whatItFakes: Which of the bill catalog's policy names read as an action the President can ask Congress for, listed by their first word.
why: The opening address needs the President's own issues as a {goal} now; the catalog names some questions as actions ("raise minimum wage") and some as things ("paid family leave"). Resolved Oct 24 (words/opening-speech-per-world): the address asks for each question by its spoken ask in data/english/question-names.json (questionTo), the same name office scenes use; the action-word list is deleted.
replacement: An action phrase on each policy question in OPUS-GOV's bill catalog, or a mined goal phrase per question from OPUS-WORDS.

whatItFakes: The register card the President's opening address composes under: election night's public-address card stands in for a President's address.
why: The engine has no register card for a State of the Union or an inaugural address yet (docs/coordination/words.md); the mined sentences need a public-address card to compose. Resolved Nov 10, 2026 (stand-in triage): dropped as too in depth (owner); the estimate stays as the game's answer.
replacement: Dropped Nov 10, 2026 (too in depth, owner): the estimate stays as the game's answer. Was: A President's-address register card in src/english/speech-registers.ts (OPUS-PEOPLE).

whatItFakes: The register card the evening news composes under: the press briefing's card stands in for a newscast.
why: Resolved Oct 28 by deletion: the opening's own newscast writer (newsStory, townStory) is gone (trim-main-every-duplicate-deleted, row W2 of docs/reports/duplicates-on-main-2026-10-28.md); the night's news is to come from the press path's stories. It stood in because the engine had no register card for a newscast (docs/coordination/words.md).
replacement: A newscast register card in src/english/speech-registers.ts (OPUS-PEOPLE).

whatItFakes: Nobody works the polling place: the election-day scene shows the voter and the household members who may vote, with no poll workers.
why: The elections engine records no polling place for a precinct and no one who works it; the scene's poll-workers role needs that record. Resolved Oct 16, 2026 (elections-poll-workers): the voting engine's pollingPlaceOf names who works each precinct's polls (named adults ranked by duty, interest in politics and free hours, as many as EAVS 2022's poll workers per voting location), and the polling-place visit carries pollingPlaceId and pollWorkerIds from it.
replacement: GOV's polling-place record (`polling-place:<precinct>` with `pollWorkerIds`), read by the poll-workers fill.

whatItFakes: How many choices a conversation turn offers: only the distinct answer moves the mined bank words, one to three per turn, with no unrelated subject tacked on to reach a count.
why: Two owner rulings pull apart: Sept 29, 'options come from context, 3 to 5 at a time'; Oct 14 (grading batch 6), a reply's second move must follow from the first. The newer one is applied until the owner rules. Resolved Oct 14 (owner ruling, afternoon): a conversation always offers four replies ranked by the player's traits (conversation.reply-reach), with 'say nothing' a smaller control beside them (sayNothing, the bench's Say nothing button); each move is offered plainly and carried on to the subject it leads to, and every acknowledgment is its own reply.
replacement: The owner's ruling: either fewer choices are right, or OPUS-WORDS mines more answer moves per subject until three to five follow naturally.

whatItFakes: How long ago a recorded event still makes something two people talk about, and lets someone not in the room be asked after.
why: The owner ruled what a talk opens on (Oct 14, 2026, night), not how long news stays news; one season is a guess checked against played talks.
replacement: A tested calibration against played talks, or an owner answer.

whatItFakes: How many days since two people last spent time together before one may say they have not seen much of the other.
why: A reading of the line in play (Amanave, American Samoa, Oct 29, 2026: "since yesterday"), not a measured quantity; a week is a guess checked against played household talks.
replacement: A tested calibration against played household talks, or an owner answer.

whatItFakes: How much the President's address weighs as a talk's topic, times the speaker's political engagement.
why: The owner ruled public news comes up only for people who follow politics closely (Oct 14, 2026, night); the size is a guess kept below a life event's. Resolved Nov 10, 2026 (stand-in triage): dropped as too in depth (owner); the estimate stays as the game's answer.
replacement: Dropped Nov 10, 2026 (too in depth, owner): the estimate stays as the game's answer. Was: A tested calibration against played talks, or an owner answer.

whatItFakes: The office scene picks its target only among members whose position reads the views engine (town bodies' full-person members); state and federal officials are skipped.
why: An official's position (officialParts) reads their officials record, not the views engine's stances, so a case made to them moves nothing. Resolved Oct 16 (director-reach): officialParts now adds the views engine's case shift to an official's own stand, and the scene no longer skips officials.
replacement: Done: officialParts reads the views engine's stance on each question (src/core2/modules/officials.ts, caseShift in views.ts), and the scene's target filter is removed; shown in src/director/office-scene-levels.test.ts.

whatItFakes: The clerk who takes a filing is left unfilled in a scene: the filing visit shows the player and the office's title, with no clerk in the room.
why: An office in the new core holds a title (the county clerk, the municipal clerk), not a person; no record names who staffs a filing counter. Resolved Oct 16 (gov-clerk-person): filingClerkFor reads an elected clerk, the town's appointed city clerk or the county government's listed clerk, and the clerk fill returns that person.
replacement: A clerk's office has a clerk: a full person on the town's payroll or an elected holder, read by the clerk fill (pool item gov-clerk-person).

whatItFakes: The person who tells someone a law changed their check is the head of the outlet whose story taught them; no record names who told them in person, and a notice from the probate court has no teller at all.
why: The news module records which story a person heard and its outlet, not who retold it. Whether a person, a friend or a reporter, should be the teller is the owner's call. Resolved Oct 19 (director-law-learned-from-outlet): the owner ruled on Oct 16 that the source is the story or feed that reached the person, so no teller is filled.
replacement: The owner's ruling: either the person who retold the story (the speech engine's retelling record) or an outlet's reporter, read by the teller fill.
resolution: Ruled by the owner on Oct 16: a person learns that a law changed their money mostly from the news or a feed, not from a person. The law-takes-effect scene is now the reached person's alone, caused by the learned-effect record, which cites the story that reached them (learnedFrom); the teller role and fill are gone, and a person is in the scene only where a conversation record shows one.

whatItFakes: What a heard speech was given at (a campaign stop, a meeting remark, a hearing), and how a candidate gave it (a town hall, a campaign speech, a debate), is read from the shape of the speech's record id, because the speech engine's record carries no occasion.
why: A mayor's remark at a council meeting was staged as a campaign event. The speech record belongs to the core area.
replacement: An occasion fact on every speech.heard record, and the campaign act on a candidate's, written by each producer (campaigns, meetings, legislature, parties, press, the governor's address), read here first.

whatItFakes: The lead below which a journal says one's own race was close.
why: A wording threshold no source sets yet; it decides only which sentence a journal may say, never an outcome. Resolved Nov 10, 2026 (stand-in triage): dropped as too in depth (owner); the estimate stays as the game's answer.
replacement: Dropped Nov 10, 2026 (too in depth, owner): the estimate stays as the game's answer. Was: A band sourced from published margin-of-victory analyses of U.S. elections.

whatItFakes: The lead above which a journal says one's own race was not close.
why: A wording threshold no source sets yet; it decides only which sentence a journal may say, never an outcome. Resolved Nov 10, 2026 (stand-in triage): dropped as too in depth (owner); the estimate stays as the game's answer.
replacement: Dropped Nov 10, 2026 (too in depth, owner): the estimate stays as the game's answer. Was: A band sourced from published margin-of-victory analyses of U.S. elections.

whatItFakes: How often a scene from circumstance may come (the days between two), how strongly it orders the journal, and how the cast is weighed (named, witnessed, the player's tie, sociability).
why: A pacing choice under the owner's Wildermyth ruling (Oct 26) with no study behind it; set so a played year in a drawn place carries scenes from circumstance about weekly while a quiet stretch carries none.
replacement: A calibration against the owner's playtests: scenes from circumstance per played month and how many he skips.

whatItFakes: A reply at home after a filing that bounds what the run may cost the household (a limit on savings, evenings kept for a child) is recorded as the reply and the time together, but no engine reads the limit.
why: The campaigns engine decides the candidate's own gifts only when the player acts, with no household limit to read; building one belongs to that engine's lead. The reply's other effects are real: the relative's yes to helping is counted among the campaign's volunteers, and a put-off lowers the tie.
replacement: A household limit the campaigns engine reads when the candidate gives their own money, with the reply naming it (pool item campaigns-household-limit-read).

whatItFakes: The clerk tells a candidate the office, the primary and general dates, the term and what the office does, but not how many petition signatures the filing needs: the clerk says nothing about signatures.
why: Owner, Oct 28 (sitting, 32, and the 2:10 PM ruling): filing is petition, signatures, the clerk's check, then the ballot. The petition record (signatures required and held, the deadline check, read from each place's rules) is the elections session's to build on its item; the words read that record once it exists. Resolved (Oct 29, 2026): once a filing is taken, the clerk says the signatures the petition record needs and the day they are due, or that the office takes no petition (filedAtCounter in src/director/filing-visit.ts, read from the elections engine's petitionOf). The signature scenes as the candidate campaigns are the next part of the plan's step 3, not a fact the clerk fakes.
replacement: The clerk's tell-signatures line reads the elections engine's petition record (signatures required, by place) and the signature scenes read its count as the candidate campaigns.

whatItFakes: A scene that ends with a favor owed or a promise made writes it on the scene's own record (facts ending and keeps), but no engine reads keeps yet: the favor is not called in and the promise is not held against the player.
why: The favor belongs to the legislature's obligations (obligationsOf) and the relationship record, the promise to the campaigns engine's promises; both engines are other leads'. Endings that strain a tie or lose trust are written to closeness now.
replacement: The legislature's keepReply and the campaigns engine read keeps (favor-owed, promise) from scene.reply and record the obligation and the promise; the journal says it from that record.

whatItFakes: At the recall table, the organizer's line that the member voted for the bill 'after telling us you wouldn't', and the member's two answers to it, need a promised-against fact; no engine records a promise to vote against a bill, so they never play and the organizer names only the vote.
why: Ask why: a broken promise is said only where a record holds the promise (a pledge, a platform stance against the bill's question, a reply in an earlier scene). The legislature records only a promise to vote for a bill (vote-promise, a committee trade).
replacement: purpose-scene sets promised-against for a recall petition when the member's filed platform takes the stand against the bill's question, or a scene reply recorded a promise against it, citing that record.

whatItFakes: A counted household evicted while counted and filled in later (the player meets one of its people) has its eviction case and housing status row, but no director moment labeled feeling:event:housing.eviction, which evictionSubjects reads; so a homeless person the player meets never brings up the eviction or where they are staying, though the records say both. A full household evicted has the moment from the day of its eviction.
why: CTO ruling, Nov 1: an evicted counted household stays counted and is filled in only when it comes to matter to the player. The director's moments are written only for watched people as events reach them, so the eviction left no moment for people not yet filled in.
replacement: When a household whose housing status row names an eviction case is filled in, the director records the eviction moment from the case (its removedAt and event id event:housing.eviction:<caseId>), or evictionSubjects reads the status row's case when no moment exists. Needs Words (lead: words).

whatItFakes: Who gives the oath at a swearing-in. Real oaths are given by a judge, a justice or a notary (a state's chief justice swears in a governor); the world keeps no courts or notaries, so the oath is given by the clerk who took the winner's filing or keeps the government's papers, else the holder who left the seat that day, else the body's presiding officer. A clerk at the state level, and every fallback, marks this stopgap.
why: Courts come after early access (AGENTS.md). Ask why: the officiant is always a person a record names (the filing clerk, the town's or county's clerk, the seat's ended term, the leadership engine's presiding officer); with none on record the scene is not staged, and no one is invented.
replacement: The justice engine's judges and justices, cast by the court that swears in each office (a chief justice for a governor, a local judge for a council), read in oathGiver ahead of the clerk.

whatItFakes: The inaugural address of a mayor, county executive or governor is recorded as heard (speech.heard) only when the player plays their own swearing-in and chooses to speak; the world's other executives give no inaugural, because the office-day engine has only the annual address. The speech's occasion is read from its record id (speech:inaugural:...), as SG-DIRECTOR-speech-occasion reads every speech's.
why: The simulation should give the address for any sworn-in executive and the scene should read it (owner, Oct 29: the player's slice of a world event). The office-day engine's acts belong to the governing lead; the scene was built against the smallest stand-in. Resolved Nov 10, 2026 (stand-in triage): dropped as too in depth (owner); the estimate stays as the game's answer.
replacement: Dropped Nov 10, 2026 (too in depth, owner): the estimate stays as the game's answer. Was: An inaugural act in the office-day engine, run for any sworn-in executive, that calls deliverSpeech with an occasion fact; the swearing-in scene then reads that record, and the existing address type stages it for the people who hear it.

whatItFakes: The counter's talk before filing (which office, the rules that stop a filing, the dates, the term and the duty) is still the filing visit's own sequence of moves, worded from the filing-clerk lines, rather than one scene of the scene engine. The clerk's talk after filing (the petition) is already the scheduled filing scene (purpose filing-petition). The filing-clerk tree lines (key routine: replies, follows and closes about a rival who filed) wait for that scene and play nowhere until then.
why: The plan approved Oct 28 (section 1) has the filing conversation fire through the one scheduler; the CTO (Nov 1, 16:05) kept the counter as the player's action screen for now and moved only the after-filing talk, so the golden path's filing step keeps working while the whole talk is built.
replacement: A filing-clerk scene, caused by the player arriving at the office that takes filings, that plays the whole counter talk through the scene engine and ends by opening the counter screen (the filing-clerk arc's endings already open it); filing-visit.ts's own sequence is then deleted.

whatItFakes: A term is read from the web's rows twelve months after the world opened, because the town's records are still settling in before that (unemployment ran 0.3 percent to 5.7 percent and poverty 9.6 percent to 18.6 percent across the first twelve months of a played year in Algiers, Vermont, seed r7). The address and the groups' reactions therefore read no area of the term in a world's first fifteen months.
why: The economy's opening state is not a settled year, so a change from it reads as the official's doing. The fix is the economy's (the start of the town's jobs and incomes), not the term read's. The school measures are fixed (a cohort too small to measure reads the place's rate, #7391).
replacement: Laws and effects (or the economy lead) start the town's jobs and poverty measures from a settled year, after which the warm-up in src/core2/data/term-read/areas.json is zero and this stopgap is removed.

whatItFakes: A strike, protest or rally is made of the named people who join it, and for the school staff's strike also of the wider town's school staff, counted and asked by the same resident decision. The wider town's renters, jobless and residents are not asked, so a protest over rent or jobs is only its named participants.
why: One model, two tiers (owner, Oct 14): a counted group is read with the same rule as a full person times its count, but the join decision (`joinsGroup`) reads a person's views, ties and traits, which a counted group does not keep one by one.
replacement: Ask the counted renters, jobless and residents by the same rule, by their count, as the school staff are, so an action's size includes every counted person who would join.

whatItFakes: A protest or strike that stands before a town official (type action-confront) is worded with the town hall's purpose (town-hall-question, reading host-declined). The narration, the protester's question, one follow and one close are the protest's own (they require the protest or strike fact); the official's replies and the endings are the town hall's, which say nothing of a crowd or a picket line.
why: The exchange is the same (a person with a demand, an official who answers) and the town hall's lines exist; the protest's own register (owner, Nov 8: the English works differently for different kinds of scenes) is the next piece of the Story lane.
replacement: A purpose of its own for action-confront in purpose-arcs.json whose replies and endings are stances toward the crowd (hear the line, send a representative, call the police, join them).

whatItFakes: How much a letter from a relative elsewhere weighs, so that a close tie's letter ranks among the year's top moments.
why: No scale item sizes a letter; the Holmes and Rahe 'change in family get-togethers' (15 units) ranks below every other moment of the year and never stages. Sized by rank in the played year (New Castle, Kentucky, seed lives-letter-a: ranks 2 to 6 of the year's moments). Resolved Nov 10, 2026 (stand-in triage): dropped as too in depth (owner); the estimate stays as the game's answer.
replacement: Dropped Nov 10, 2026 (too in depth, owner): the estimate stays as the game's answer. Was: A measured weight of family contact in the life-change literature, or the people engine's own appraisal of the contact.

whatItFakes: A group's lobbyist who remembers how the player voted (circumstance lobby-remembers) says so, subtle or open by their own temper, and what the player answers is kept as a promise or a strained tie. The group's endorsement, gifts or a primary challenge do not move from it: the interest-group engine does not read the tie or the kept answer when it decides whom to back.
why: The threat is told and kept in the records the director already writes; making the group's backing follow the member's votes is the interest-group engine's decision, which no engine yet reads from a vote against the group (Laws and effects' area).
replacement: The interest-group engine reads the member's vote against its meeting and the kept tie when it decides endorsements and gifts; the scene then cites that decision.

whatItFakes: How much each read of the records (the size of a bribe against the official's year, the tie, the offerer's need, earlier refusals and pressure, where the scene is set; for a donor's ask, the gift against the donor's own year, its share of what others gave, how close the two are, earlier gifts and earlier asks the candidate put off; for a reporter's call, how far the town's shares stand against the member's vote, earlier talks the two had, a quarrel on their tie, stories of scandal against the member, and the reporter's outlet with the bill's level; for an apology owed after a quarrel over a missed payment, whether the quarrel is about money, how close the two are, earlier quarrels between them and the wronged person's own money pressure; for an accusation after a complaint to the prosecutor, whether the accuser saw the offer or was told of it, whether the bribe was taken and how close the two are) counts toward each variant of a scene, and how much each variant's facets pull the asker to it.
why: The mechanism is data and the reads are real records, but the weights are set by hand against the spread of reads in drawn places (Nov 8, Story session) so that every variant wins somewhere in play; no study sizes how much a small gift or a repeated ask differs in the way people go about it. They stay TUNABLE against play and the owner's voice notes. Gaps in the press-comment reads (Nov 9, Story session): the town's view is the electorate's shares on the bill's question (voting.ts electorateSides), which read nothing for a question the survey has no item for, so a vote on such a bill never reads as against the town; no record keeps an outlet's lean toward the member, so a hostile reporter is read from the town, earlier quarrels and the tie alone; press.snubbed and press.attacked name the outlet's staff but not who snubbed them in their people, so they are not read; no record keeps an accusation that the press has not printed, so a chase is read from reported bribes, convictions and press.exposed stories (the last half year); the national press is the reporter's outlet tier (only federal bills cast national reporters) and a state bill reaches it only through the level read; a call about a bill held in committee has no vote of the member's to read. Resolved Nov 10, 2026 (stand-in triage): dropped as too in depth (owner); the estimate stays as the game's answer.
replacement: Dropped Nov 10, 2026 (too in depth, owner): the estimate stays as the game's answer. Was: Weights fitted to how often real bribe approaches are small, large, from a friend, repeated or desperate (the corruption literature's cases), checked against the played years, or read straight from the corruption engine's own reasons once it keeps one for each.

whatItFakes: The adviser in the advice scene (the day after a party's chair asks the player to run) is a seated officeholder of that party who lives in the player's town and has held a seat for a year or more, the closest and most sociable of them. replacement: Dropped Nov 10, 2026 (too in depth, owner): the estimate stays as the game's answer. Was: The moves engine records the one cause that tipped the pull over the holds (the largest term on a common scale) on the departure; the farewell reads that.

whatItFakes: The talk over a damaged home (circumstance home-damaged) is cast only from the people who live with the player. replacement: Dropped Nov 10, 2026 (too in depth, owner): the estimate stays as the game's answer. Was: The moment records the minute its setting opened it (ledger openedAt) and composeScene reads that.

whatItFakes: How strongly a speaker's traits tilt a governor's or mayor's address toward a kind. The mean of the kind's facet values is clamped to -1..1 though the facets run past it (a work-centered, meticulous governor's mean is 1.2), and the policy kind's base (policyBase 0.5, times the full agenda) doubles at the cap, so a speaker with a full list of asks and a work-centered turn scores policy 1.0 against a collapsing term's crisis 0.656 and gives the same address in a good term and a bad one (Greensboro, Maryland, seed f8fc37cc25201edc, official:term:seat:US-MD:governor:2025-01-20).
why: Calibration, not a clamp on the score: the policy score is raw (0.5 x work share x (1 + pull)) and, even unclamped (pull 1.2, score 1.1), is above crisis. Whether a full-agenda governor should still name a collapsing term is a Words call on policyBase, the pull scale and the crisis weight, which the owner has not ruled. Resolved Nov 10, 2026 (stand-in triage): dropped as too in depth (owner); the estimate stays as the game's answer.
replacement: Dropped Nov 10, 2026 (too in depth, owner): the estimate stays as the game's answer. Was: Words checks the address kinds against real State of the State addresses (a crisis term outweighs a long agenda), then sets policyBase and the pull's scale so a bad term can outscore policy for any speaker.

whatItFakes: The homecoming scene's ending (you settled what comes next, by agreeing to a stay or promising to help find work) is written on the reply record as a promise; no engine reads it. replacement: Dropped Nov 10, 2026 (too in depth, owner): the estimate stays as the game's answer. Was: A justice-engine account for a named prisoner that a promise of money pays into on the next day, and a people-engine owed-talk record for the word taken to the family.

replacement: Dropped Nov 10, 2026 (too in depth, owner): the estimate stays as the game's answer. Was: Memberships for congregations and clubs, and an address on the household record; meeting-facts.ts then reads them as it reads the party.

whatItFakes: What the player agrees to or promises in the introduction (to show the newcomer around) or the friend's ask (to come along, to do the favor) is written on the reply record as a promise; no engine moves the tie, makes the day's plan or does the favor beyond the contact hours every reply writes.

replacement: A people-engine plan or owed-talk record that reads a kept promise on these two types and brings the player and the missing relative together, and kin contact that rises after a kept call or visit.

whatItFakes: What the housemate who got the player help asks afterward (a ride to the doctor, a visit to one, to stay close, a promise to say when the player feels sick again, leave to tell the family, a word with a child who was in the room) is worded for every rescue; nothing on a record says this rescuer wants a visit to the doctor. whatItFakes: A job found, lost or left is told as a small story from the past-work records. An official's referral is on record and employers read it, but the hire keeps no referral, so the entry never says who helped, and the feeling in it is only what the pay comparison supports.

whatItFakes: The outline rows for a campaign speech, a floor speech, a victory, a concession and a swearing-in exist, but those speeches are still worded by their own paths (speech-builder.ts, wordSpeechPart, single scene lines) and do not go through planSpeech, because their banks hold no pieces by section.

whatItFakes: The theme weights (speech-outlines.json theme) are first guesses: in ten drawn worlds on Nov 12 the President's address led with paying for a higher debt limit in six, because the macro year is nearly the same in every world and the taxes-finance subject holds the one open federal question most Presidents stand far from the center on.

whatItFakes: The rent coming due is read from the lease a household signed when the world was made (`lease:<household>`); a lease signed after a move (`lease:<household>:<date>`) is not found, so a household that moved never talks about its rent.

whatItFakes: A jobless housemate says nothing of looking for work: the jobs engine (src/core2/modules/jobs.ts) keeps job offers only for the person the player controls, and a jobless adult out of the labor force has no seeker row, so no application, interview, rejection or benefit paid is on record to tell.

whatItFakes: What a government did (a budget line, an ordinance, an address, a town hall) is told as news the speaker heard or read, citing that record, with their stand on its question; whether it reached their own household (a service they use, a tax they pay, a payroll they are on) is not read, so nobody says it touched them.
why: The town changing, brought up at home (lead, Nov 12), built on the records the speaker has (the story read, the address heard, the meeting attended); the budget and benefits engines' records of whom a line served are not read by talk yet.
replacement: Talk reads the budget, benefits and tax engines' records of whom a changed line reached, and a speaker it reached gives that as their reason.
